implementation_notes: JavaScript has no built-in authorization: the guard is a higher-order function - guard(policy) returning a (req, res, next) function - mounted on the routes or wrapped around an operation, and the policy is a plain module of pure decision functions such as canEdit(user, doc) returning a structured result. What replaces the classic structure: functions returning functions (middleware) replace Guard objects and a frozen policy module replaces the Policy class; the subject and its attributes come from the server-side session or JWT, and when they must reach deep async call chains, from an AsyncLocalStorage store created by the authentication middleware. The classic object form gains nothing here - the only reason to introduce a class is to hold configuration, and a closure does that with less ceremony.
idiom_name: higher-order guard function (middleware) + pure policy module
pitfalls: Middleware order is the enforcement contract: a route registered before the guard, or an error path that bypasses it, is an unprotected route - consider a global guard plus explicit public routes.

AsyncLocalStorage stores do not always cross worker threads, some third-party callbacks or event-emitter boundaries; when getStore() returns undefined the guard must deny rather than treat the call as anonymous-with-rights.
Never derive the subject or its roles from client-supplied body or query fields; the guard must read the server-side session or verified token only.
